summary:
LongMemEval ("LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory", Di Wu, Hongwei Wang, Wenhao Yu, Yuwei Zhang, Kai-Wei Chang, Dong Yu; ICLR 2025; arXiv 2410.10813; OpenReview pZiyCaVuti) is the de-facto standard benchmark for long-term conversational memory. It contains 500 manually curated questions, each embedded in a freely scalable, timestamped user-assistant chat history ("haystack") built by an attribute-controlled pipeline in the needle-in-a-haystack style. It tests five core abilities: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention.

DATA FORMAT: each of the 500 instances is a JSON object with fields: `question_id` (unique id; if it ends with `_abs` the question is an abstention/false-premise question — 30 such instances exist, drawn from the other types and modified into false-premise form), `question_type` (one of six labels: single-session-user, single-session-assistant, single-session-preference, temporal-reasoning, knowledge-update, multi-session; abstention is the implicit seventh type marked only via the `_abs` id suffix, giving "seven types"), `question`, `answer`, `question_date` (timestamp of the question — essential for query-conditioned temporal reasoning), `haystack_session_ids`, `haystack_dates` (per-session timestamps), `haystack_sessions` (list of sessions; each session is a list of turns `{"role": "user"|"assistant", "content": ...}`, and evidence turns additionally carry `"has_answer": true`), and `answer_session_ids` (ground-truth evidence session ids used for memory-recall evaluation). Per-type counts (sum = 500): single-session-user 70, single-session-assistant 56, single-session-preference 30, multi-session 133, knowledge-update 78, temporal-reasoning 133; 30 abstention instances overlap these labels via `_abs` ids.

VARIANTS: (1) longmemeval_s ("S"): ~115k tokens of history per question (~40-50 sessions, tokenized with Llama 3); HF file ~277-278 MB. (2) longmemeval_m ("M"): ~500 sessions per history, roughly 1.5M tokens; HF file ~2.74-2.75 GB. (3) longmemeval_oracle: only the evidence sessions are included (oracle retrieval); 15.4 MB. All three contain the same 500 questions. A cleaned re-release (2025/09) "further cleaned up the history sessions to prevent interference on answer correctness" and is the currently recommended version (files longmemeval_s_cleaned.json, longmemeval_m_cleaned.json, longmemeval_oracle.json in the xiaowu0162/longmemeval-cleaned HF repo).

EVALUATION PROTOCOL: generation systems write a JSONL hypothesis file with fields `question_id` and `hypothesis` per line; `src/evaluation/evaluate_qa.py <judge_model> <hypothesis_file> <reference_file>` calls an LLM judge (paper uses gpt-4o-2024-08-06; script supports gpt-4o / gpt-4o-mini / llama-3.1-70b-instruct; temperature 0, max 10 tokens) with QUESTION-TYPE-SPECIFIC binary yes/no prompts, then `print_qa_metrics.py` aggregates accuracy overall and per type (the judge decision is parsed as `'yes' in eval_response.lower()`, producing an `autoeval_label`). Per-type judge-prompt logic: default types — answer must contain the correct answer, subsets count as wrong; temporal-reasoning — off-by-one errors in day/week/month counts are not penalized; knowledge-update — response is correct if it contains the updated answer even if old info is also mentioned; single-session-preference — graded against a rubric, but "does not need to reflect all the points in the rubric"; abstention (`_abs`) — judged yes iff the model identifies the question as unanswerable/information-missing. The paper reports >97% judge-human agreement. Retrieval is evaluated separately with Recall@k and NDCG@k at `turn` or `session` granularity (`run_retrieval.sh IN_FILE RETRIEVER GRANULARITY`, retrievers flat-bm25 / flat-contriever / flat-stella / flat-gte; `print_retrieval_metrics.py`; ground truth = answer_session_ids and has_answer flags; retrieval metrics skip the 30 abstention instances). The paper also proposes memory-design optimizations across indexing/retrieval/reading: session decomposition, fact-augmented key expansion, time-aware query expansion (key-expansion outputs downloadable from Google Drive links in the README).

PAPER BASELINE RESULTS: long-context full-history reading on S vs oracle: GPT-4o 0.870 (oracle) → 0.606 (S), a 30.3% relative drop; Llama 3.1 70B 0.744 → 0.334 (55.1% drop); Phi-3 14B 0.702 → 0.380. Commercial assistants on histories ~10x shorter than S: ChatGPT (GPT-4o) 37% drop, Coze 64% drop vs offline reading.

SOTA 2025-2026 (mostly vendor self-reported, on longmemeval_s, GPT-4o judge unless noted; NOT strictly comparable — different dataset versions (original vs cleaned), judges, and answer models): Zep (arXiv 2501.13956, Jan 2025): 71.2% with gpt-4o (vs 60.2% full-context), 63.8% with gpt-4o-mini (vs 55.4%); latency 2.58s vs 28.9s, ~1.6k context tokens vs 115k; per-type gpt-4o: SSU 92.9, SSA 80.4, SSP 56.7, TR 62.4, KU 83.3, MS 57.9. Emergence AI (blog, June 2025): 86% overall with improved session-level RAG + cross-encoder rerank + CoT (SSA 100, SSU 98.57, TR 85.71, KU 83.33, MS 81.20, SSP 60), vs Oracle GPT-4o 82.4%; "Simple Fast" variant 79%. Mastra (blog, Jul 2025): 80% with plain semantic recall topK-20 + date-grouped formatting (SSA 100, SSU 97.1, KU 84.6, MS 76.7, TR 75.2, SSP 46.7); a later Mastra figure of 94.87% circulates on third-party leaderboards. Supermemory (research page): claims ~95% overall (SSU 97, SSA 100, SSP 90, KU 99, TR 91, MS 93), Zep numbers copied from Zep's paper. Mem0 (research page + 2026 blogs): 94.4 overall at ~6.8k mean retrieval tokens (per-category numbers reported inconsistently across their pages, e.g., blog: SSU 98.6/SSA 98.2/KU 93.6/MS 88.0). ByteRover 2.1.5 (blog): 92.8% on LongMemEval-S at 1.6s latency. OMEGA (omegamax.co leaderboard, Feb 2026): 95.4% (466/500) but with GPT-4.1 as generator AND judge (nonstandard). Fringe self-reported GitHub claims: agentmemory 96.2% (481/500), MemPalace/MemPal ~96.6%. Letta publishes no LongMemEval score. LONGMEMEVAL-V2 (2026/05, arXiv 2605.12493, github.com/xiaowu0162/LongMemEval-V2, HF xiaowu0162/longmemeval-v2): shifts to agentic memory — 451 questions over multimodal web-agent trajectory haystacks (up to 500 trajectories / 115M tokens), abilities: static state recall, dynamic state tracking, workflow knowledge, environment gotchas, premise awareness; leaderboard metric "LAFS Gain" rewards the accuracy-latency frontier.
benchmark_details: Instance schema (all three variants share it): question_id (string; `_abs` suffix marks the 30 abstention/false-premise questions), question_type ∈ {single-session-user, single-session-assistant, single-session-preference, temporal-reasoning, knowledge-update, multi-session}, question (string), answer (string), question_date (timestamp string of when the question is asked), haystack_session_ids (list), haystack_dates (list of per-session timestamps, aligned with haystack_session_ids), haystack_sessions (list of sessions; each session = list of {"role": "user"/"assistant", "content": str} turns; evidence turns carry extra "has_answer": true), answer_session_ids (list of ground-truth evidence session ids). Sizes: 500 questions in every variant. longmemeval_s ≈ 115k history tokens/question (~40-50 sessions; Llama-3 tokenizer), HF file 277-278 MB; longmemeval_m ≈ 500 sessions (~1.5M tokens), HF file 2.74-2.75 GB; longmemeval_oracle = evidence sessions only, 15.4 MB. Per-type counts: SSU 70, SSA 56, SSP 30, MS 133, KU 78, TR 133 (sum 500); 30 abstention instances distributed across types via `_abs` ids. Official metrics: (a) QA accuracy via LLM judge — hypothesis JSONL {question_id, hypothesis} → `python3 src/evaluation/evaluate_qa.py gpt-4o hyp_file data/longmemeval_oracle.json` (judge gpt-4o-2024-08-06 in the paper, temperature 0, max 10 tokens, binary yes/no parsed by substring 'yes'; >97% human agreement) → `print_qa_metrics.py` for overall + per-type accuracy; per-type judge rules: TR forgives off-by-one date arithmetic; KU accepts updated answer even when stale info is co-mentioned; SSP uses a rubric but partial rubric coverage is OK; `_abs` judged correct iff model abstains/says unanswerable; default types require the full correct answer (subset = wrong). (b) Memory recall: Recall@k and NDCG@k at turn or session granularity against answer_session_ids / has_answer (abstention instances skipped); baseline retrievers flat-bm25, flat-contriever, flat-stella, flat-gte via `bash run_retrieval.sh IN_FILE RETRIEVER GRANULARITY`, metrics via `print_retrieval_metrics.py`. Repo layout: data/, src/evaluation/ (evaluate_qa.py, print_qa_metrics.py, print_retrieval_metrics.py), src/retrieval/, src/generation/, generation_logs/.

sota_numbers: Paper baselines (S variant, GPT-4o judge): GPT-4o full-context 60.6% vs oracle 87.0% (30.3% drop); Llama-3.1-70B 33.4% vs 74.4%; ChatGPT 37% drop / Coze 64% drop on shorter histories [arXiv 2410.10813]. Zep (Jan 2025, arXiv 2501.13956): gpt-4o 71.2% (vs 60.2% full-context), gpt-4o-mini 63.8% (vs 55.4%); 2.58s vs 28.9s latency; per-type gpt-4o SSU 92.9 / SSA 80.4 / SSP 56.7 / TR 62.4 / KU 83.3 / MS 57.9. Emergence AI (Jun 2025 blog): 86% overall (SSA 100, SSU 98.57, TR 85.71, KU 83.33, MS 81.20, SSP 60), Oracle GPT-4o 82.4%, naive RAG 52% [emergence.ai/blog/sota-on-longmemeval-with-rag]. Mastra (Jul 2025 blog): 80% (semantic recall topK 20); third-party leaderboards later list Mastra at 94.87% [mastra.ai/blog/use-rag-for-agent-memory; omegamax.co/benchmarks]. Supermemory (self-reported research page): ~95% overall; SSU 97, SSA 100, SSP 90, KU 99, TR 91, MS 93 [supermemory.ai/research/longmembench/]. Mem0 (self-reported, 2026): 94.4 overall at ~6,787 mean retrieval tokens; per-category figures inconsistent across their own pages [mem0.ai/research; mem0.ai/blog/ai-memory-benchmarks-in-2026]. ByteRover 2.1.5 (self-reported): 92.8% on LongMemEval-S, 1.6s latency [byterover.dev blog]. OMEGA (Feb 2026, nonstandard GPT-4.1 judge+generator): 95.4% (466/500) [omegamax.co/benchmarks]. Unverified GitHub claims: agentmemory 96.2% (481/500), MemPal/MemPalace ~96.6%. Letta: no published LongMemEval score. Caveat: numbers span original vs cleaned datasets, different judges and answer models, and are mostly vendor self-reported — no neutral leaderboard exists for V1.
gaps_for_qvf: LongMemEval evaluates only two endpoints — retrieval recall (Recall@k/NDCG@k vs answer_session_ids) and final QA accuracy (binary LLM judge) — with NOTHING in between: exactly the post-retrieval / pre-generation slot QVF occupies. Concrete gaps QVF can fill: (1) No claim-level or relation-level ground truth — the benchmark never labels which retrieved memories contradict, supersede, or merely coexist with each other; QVF's Validity Map (EQUIVALENT/SUPPORTS/CONTRADICTS/SUPERSEDES/...) is a new annotation and evaluation layer, and knowledge-update questions (78) plus temporal-reasoning questions (133) give natural weak supervision: the update chain and question_date allow deriving SUPERSEDED_FOR_QUERY vs CURRENT_FOR_QUERY vs HISTORICAL_FOR_QUERY labels programmatically from answer_session_ids + haystack_dates. (2) Query-conditioned validity is the benchmark's hardest failure mode but is untested directly: temporal-reasoning is the weakest category for nearly every system (Zep 62.4, Mastra 75.2, Emergence 85.71, full-context GPT-4o 45.1), and Mem0's own blog admits ADD-only architectures degrade on knowledge-update — yet no metric distinguishes 'retrieved the right memory but misjudged its validity for this query' from 'never retrieved it'. QVF can define this decomposition (retrieval error vs validity-judgment error vs reading error) as a new diagnostic metric. (3) Abstention is marginal in LongMemEval (only 30 `_abs` instances, skipped in retrieval metrics, judged with a single yes/no prompt); QVF's sufficiency assessment (SUFFICIENT/INSUFFICIENT/AMBIGUOUS) generalizes abstention into calibrated sufficiency and can be validated on the `_abs` subset (INSUFFICIENT should predict abstention) while extending it with risk flags the benchmark lacks. (4) The judge protocol is per-type binary with no partial credit and no explanation audit — QVF's structured, citation-carrying claims enable attributable evaluation (which memory-IDs justified the answer) that the official protocol cannot express. (5) The distractor dimension is implicit (filler sessions from 5_filler_sess) but never scored; QVF's DISTRACTOR/UNRELATED roles make it explicit. (6) Practically: use longmemeval_s_cleaned.json as the main testbed (115k tokens fits standard retrieval budgets; M variant stresses scale), keep the official GPT-4o judge for end-to-end comparability with Zep/Emergence/Supermemory/Mem0 numbers, and report the standard per-type accuracy PLUS QVF's new intermediate metrics; also note V1 saturation claims (94-96% self-reported) motivate QVF's finer-grained evaluation story, and LongMemEval-V2 (agentic, premise awareness) is a plausible future extension target.

papers.title: LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory
papers.core_idea: 500 curated questions embedded in scalable timestamped chat histories testing information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention; shows 30%+ accuracy drops for long-context LLMs and commercial assistants; proposes session decomposition, fact-augmented key expansion, and time-aware query expansion.
papers.relation_to_qvf: QVF's primary evaluation benchmark. Its question_date + haystack_dates + answer_session_ids + has_answer fields provide exactly the metadata QVF's Semantic Adapter consumes, and its knowledge-update/temporal-reasoning/abstention types map directly onto QVF's temporal labels, SUPERSEDES relation, and sufficiency assessment. But it only scores retrieval recall and final QA accuracy — QVF adds the missing intermediate validity layer.

papers.title: Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory
papers.core_idea: Graphiti, a temporally-aware knowledge graph memory engine; 71.2% on LongMemEval-S with gpt-4o (vs 60.2% full-context) at 90% lower latency using ~1.6k context tokens.
papers.relation_to_qvf: Closest philosophical neighbor: encodes temporal validity (fact valid-from/invalid-at edges) at INGESTION time into a graph. QVF differs by computing validity QUERY-CONDITIONED at read time — an 'invalidated' fact can still be CURRENT_FOR_QUERY for a historical question, which Zep's global edge invalidation cannot express.

papers.title: SOTA on LongMemEval with RAG (EmergenceMem)
papers.core_idea: 86% on LongMemEval-S via turn-level matching with session-level retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, and chain-of-thought answering — beating Oracle GPT-4o (82.4%).
papers.relation_to_qvf: Shows careful retrieval + CoT alone reaches 86%, but per-type numbers (SSP 60%, KU 83%) reveal residual errors in preference and update handling — the validity-judgment errors QVF targets; a strong baseline to ablate against.

papers.title: Zep Is The New State of the Art In Agent Memory
papers.core_idea: Marketing companion to the Zep paper; details the LongMemEval-S setup (top-20 edges/nodes retrieved from the knowledge graph).
papers.relation_to_qvf: Documents the retrieval configuration (k=20 facts) that most later vendor comparisons copied; useful for standardizing QVF's retrieval budget.

papers.title: LongMemEval — Supermemory Research
papers.core_idea: Claims ~95% overall on LongMemEval-S with ~720 added tokens; per-type SSU 97 / SSA 100 / SSP 90 / KU 99 / TR 91 / MS 93; Zep comparison numbers taken from Zep's paper, not re-run.
papers.relation_to_qvf: Illustrates benchmark saturation claims and the comparability problem (no shared judge/protocol); motivates QVF's finer-grained, attributable intermediate metrics.

papers.title: Mem0 Research: Token-Efficient Memory (2026 scores)
papers.core_idea: Claims 94.4 on LongMemEval and 92.5 on LoCoMo at ~6.8-7.0k mean tokens per retrieval; admits ADD-only (no update/delete) architecture hurts knowledge-update and multi-session categories.
papers.relation_to_qvf: Their acknowledged weakness — stale memories accumulating without supersession handling — is precisely the failure QVF's SUPERSEDES relation and query-conditioned temporal labels address.

papers.title: Yes, you can use RAG for agent memory
papers.core_idea: 80% on longmemeval_s with plain vector recall (topK 20) plus date-grouped message formatting; argues simple RAG with good temporal formatting rivals graph memories.
papers.relation_to_qvf: Evidence that surfacing timestamps to the reader model matters — QVF systematizes this by converting raw timestamps into explicit query-conditioned temporal labels rather than relying on the generator to infer them.

papers.title: LongMemEval-V2: Evaluating Long-Term Agent Memory in Agentic Context
papers.core_idea: 451 questions over multimodal web-agent trajectory haystacks (up to 500 trajectories / 115M tokens); abilities: static state recall, dynamic state tracking, workflow knowledge, environment gotchas, premise awareness; LAFS-Gain leaderboard metric rewards the accuracy-latency frontier.
papers.relation_to_qvf: Successor benchmark from the same authors; its 'premise awareness' and 'dynamic state tracking' abilities are agentic analogues of QVF's sufficiency assessment and temporal validity — a natural future-work target after LongMemEval V1 + LoCoMo.

papers.title: OMEGA LongMemEval Benchmark Leaderboard
papers.core_idea: Aggregates published scores (OMEGA 95.4 with GPT-4.1 judge, Mastra 94.87, Emergence 86, Zep 71.2) and notes most memory vendors (Mem0 per-type, Letta, Claude native) do not publish LongMemEval scores.
papers.relation_to_qvf: Best single snapshot of the fragmented 2026 'leaderboard'; underlines that no neutral protocol exists — QVF experiments should pin dataset version (cleaned), judge (gpt-4o), and retrieval budget explicitly.

summary:
LoCoMo ("Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents", Maharana, Lee, Tulyakov, Bansal, Barbieri, Fang; ACL 2024 Long Papers, 2024.acl-long.747; arXiv:2402.17753) is a machine-generated + human-edited benchmark of very long multi-session dyadic conversations between two LLM-simulated personas (personas seeded from MSC, released as data/msc_personas_all.json; conversations grounded in temporal event graphs, with image sharing where turns carry img_url + BLIP captions). PAPER-VERSION STATS (50 conversations): avg 19.3 sessions, 304.9 turns, ~9,209 tokens per conversation, up to 35 sessions over months; 7,512 QA pairs across 5 categories: single-hop 2,705 (36%), multi-hop 1,104 (14.6%), temporal reasoning 1,547 (20.6%), open-domain knowledge 285 (3.9%), adversarial 1,871 (24.9%). RELEASED VERSION (what everyone actually uses): data/locomo10.json in github.com/snap-research/locomo — only 10 conversations, 1,986 QA pairs; per-category counts: category 4 = 841 (42.3%), category 5 = 446 (22.5%), category 2 = 321 (16.2%), category 1 = 282 (14.2%), category 3 = 96 (4.8%). Excluding category 5 leaves the widely cited 1,540 questions.

DATA FORMAT (verified by fetching the raw locomo10.json): top level is a JSON list of conversation samples. Each sample has keys: "qa" (list) and "conversation" (object), plus in the repo README-documented annotations "event_summary" (events_session_<n> per speaker, ground truth for the event-summarization task), "observation" (session_<n>_observation, generated facts used as a RAG database), and "session_summary" (session_<n>_summary, generated summaries used as another RAG database), and "sample_id". "conversation" contains: speaker_a, speaker_b, and paired keys session_<n> (list of turns) and session_<n>_date_time (natural-language timestamp string like "1:56 pm on 8 May, 2023" — NOT ISO; any temporal system must parse these). Each turn has: speaker, dia_id (e.g. "D1:3" = session 1, dialog 3), text, and optionally img_url, blip_caption (and a search query used to fetch the image). Each qa item has: question, answer (string or number), evidence (list of dia_id strings like ["D1:3","D7:11"] — ground-truth supporting turns), category (int 1–5); category-5 items have "adversarial_answer" INSTEAD of a normal answer field.

CATEGORY NUMBERING — CRITICAL TRAP: per the original paper taxonomy matched to the released counts and question styles, the data numbering is: 1 = multi-hop (282), 2 = temporal reasoning (321), 3 = open-domain/counterfactual ("Would X still ... if ..." style, 96), 4 = single-hop (841), 5 = adversarial/unanswerable (446). However, the Mem0 evaluation harness (which Memobase, Backboard and most later vendor evals forked) hardcodes categories = ["single_hop","temporal","multi_hop","open_domain"] indexed 1..4 — i.e., it calls category 1 "single_hop", category 3 "multi_hop", and category 4 "open_domain". So per-category columns in Mem0-lineage tables are MISLABELED relative to the paper taxonomy (only "temporal" matches); e.g., Mem0's high "open-domain" scores are actually on the 841 single-hop questions, and its low "multi-hop" scores are on the 96 open-domain counterfactuals. Multiple sources document this paper-vs-code mapping mismatch; use counts (282/321/96/841/446) to disambiguate any published table.

ORIGINAL EVALUATION (task_eval/evaluation.py + paper): QA scored by token-level F1 with answer normalization (lowercase, strip articles/punctuation, Porter stemming); category 1 (multi-hop) answers are comma-split and scored with a partial multi-answer F1; categories 2/3/4 use plain F1; category 5 scored binarily by checking whether the output contains "no information available" or "not mentioned" (models are prompted to say "No information available" for unanswerable questions). Also implemented: exact match, ROUGE-L, BERTScore. Retrieval quality measured by recall@k over three RAG databases (raw dialogs, observations, session summaries). Event summarization: ROUGE-1/2/L + FactScore precision/recall/F1. Multimodal dialogue generation: MMRelevance (evaluation code for these two tasks was never fully released — "Coming soon"). Headline paper results: best QA overall ≈37.8% F1 (GPT-3.5-turbo-16K family baselines; humans 87.9% F1; temporal reasoning worst at ~20.3% vs human 92.6%); long-context and RAG variants (scripts/evaluate_rag_gpts.sh, top-k ∈ {5,10,25,50}) still far below human.

LATER-PAPER EVALUATION (de-facto standard since Mem0, arXiv:2504.19413): generate answers with gpt-4o-mini from retrieved memories, score with F1, BLEU-1, and "J" = LLM-as-a-Judge (binary correct/wrong; Mem0 used gpt-4o-mini as judge with lenient instructions returning JSON; Memobase used gpt-4o) on categories 1–4 only (adversarial excluded, claimed "ground truth unavailable" — actually because category-5 rows have adversarial_answer, and the original abstention-scoring was never ported). Mem0 paper J scores (10 runs avg): Mem0 66.88 (per-category as labeled by them: single-hop 67.13, multi-hop 51.15, temporal 55.51, open-domain 72.93), Mem0-graph 68.44, Zep 65.99, LangMem 58.10, OpenAI Memory 52.90, A-Mem lower (e.g. 39.79 single-hop), full-context baseline 72.90 (i.e., FULL CONTEXT BEATS ALL MEMORY SYSTEMS); latency: Mem0 search p95 0.200s, total p95 1.440s vs full-context total p95 17.117s (the "91% lower p95 latency" claim).

CONTROVERSIES: (1) Mem0-vs-Zep war: Zep's rebuttal blog ("Lies, Damn Lies, Statistics: Is Mem0 Really SOTA?") says Mem0 misconfigured Zep (both speakers ingested as the same user role; timestamps appended to message text instead of Zep's created_at field; sequential instead of parallel searches) and reports corrected Zep J = 75.14% ± 0.17, p95 search 0.632s; Mem0's CTO countered in getzep/zep-papers issue #5 that Zep's later "84%" claim counted adversarial correct answers in the numerator but not denominator, changed prompts/templates, and used a single run, computing 58.44% ± 0.20 under Mem0's standardized protocol. (2) Benchmark-quality audit (Penfield Labs / dial481-locomo-audit, 2026): 99/1,540 (6.4%) wrong golden answers → effective score ceiling ~93.6% (per-category ceilings e.g. single-hop 95.72%, multi-hop 90.07%), LLM judge accepts up to ~63% of intentionally wrong vague-but-topical answers, category 5 (446 questions) has never been evaluated in any published memory-system result, tiny open-domain n=96 needs ~15-point gaps for significance, and 56% of adjacent leaderboard comparisons are statistically indistinguishable; some vendor claims (e.g. EverMemOS 95.96% single-hop) exceed the mathematical ceiling, implying credit from wrong gold answers. (3) Letta's blog shows a trivial filesystem-memory agent on gpt-4o-mini scores 74.0%, arguing LoCoMo is nearly saturated and doesn't discriminate memory architectures. (4) Zep and others note conversations (~16k–26k tokens) fit in modern context windows and the benchmark has NO knowledge-update/supersession questions — they advocate LongMemEval for that. (5) Scores across vendors are not comparable: different judges (gpt-4o vs gpt-4o-mini), prompts, retrieval configs, single-run vs 10-run averaging, and the category-label swap. Newer vendor numbers under their own harnesses: Memobase v0.0.37 75.78 J; Mem0's 2026 algorithm claims LoCoMo 92.5 (avg 6,956 tokens/query) and LongMemEval 94.4 — self-reported, post-audit-era caveats apply. A multiple-choice re-release exists: HuggingFace Percena/locomo-mc10 (all 1,986 questions as 10-option MC with fields question/choices/correct_choice_index/question_type + haystack_sessions/haystack_session_summaries/haystack_session_datetimes) to replace LLM-judge with plain accuracy.

papers.title: Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents (LoCoMo)
papers.core_idea: Machine-generated + human-verified very-long multi-session persona dialogues (paper: 50 convs, avg 304.9 turns / 9.2k tokens / 19.3 sessions; released: 10 convs) with three tasks: QA over 5 question categories (single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, adversarial; F1 with stemming/normalization, comma-split partial F1 for multi-hop, abstention-phrase check for adversarial), event summarization (ROUGE + FactScore), and multimodal dialog generation (MMRelevance); shows GPT-3.5/GPT-4-era models far below human F1 (37.8 vs 87.9 overall; worst on temporal).
papers.relation_to_qvf: QVF's planned generalization benchmark. Its evidence field (dia_id lists) gives free ground truth for QVF's memory-ID citations (citation precision/recall); its category 5 adversarial questions map directly to QVF's DISTRACTOR role + INSUFFICIENT sufficiency output; its NL timestamps ("1:56 pm on 8 May, 2023") stress QVF's query-conditioned temporal labels. But it has no supersession/knowledge-update questions, so QVF's SUPERSEDED_FOR_QUERY machinery must be validated mainly on LongMemEval.

papers.title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
papers.core_idea: Extraction+update memory pipeline (and graph variant Mem0-g); established the now-standard LoCoMo protocol for memory systems: categories 1–4 only (1,540 Qs), gpt-4o-mini answerer, metrics F1/BLEU-1/LLM-as-a-Judge (gpt-4o-mini, binary, lenient), 10-run averages; J: Mem0 66.88, Mem0-g 68.44, Zep 65.99, LangMem 58.10, OpenAI Memory 52.90, full-context 72.90; big latency wins vs full-context (total p95 1.44s vs 17.1s).
papers.relation_to_qvf: Defines the evaluation harness QVF should reuse for comparability (and whose category-label swap QVF must correct when reporting per-category numbers). Mem0 filters/compresses at WRITE time; QVF filters at READ time conditioned on the query — complementary, and QVF can be layered on top of Mem0-style retrieval. Full-context beating all memory systems here is the gap QVF targets: better post-retrieval reasoning rather than more retrieval.

papers.title: Is Mem0 Really SOTA in Agent Memory? (Zep rebuttal)
papers.core_idea: Claims Mem0 misconfigured Zep on LoCoMo (both speakers as one user; timestamps in message text not created_at; sequential search) and reports corrected Zep J = 75.14% ± 0.17, p95 search 0.632s; also attacks LoCoMo itself (fits in context windows, no knowledge-update questions, unusable category 5, speaker-attribution and multimodal errors) and endorses LongMemEval (~115k-token conversations).
papers.relation_to_qvf: Documents exactly the metadata-handling pitfalls QVF's Semantic Adapter must avoid (timestamps as first-class metadata, correct speaker attribution). Its critique that LoCoMo lacks update/supersession questions justifies QVF's LongMemEval-main / LoCoMo-generalization split.

papers.title: Revisiting Zep's 84% LoCoMo Claim: Corrected Evaluation & 58.44% Accuracy (zep-papers issue #5)
papers.venue: GitHub issue (filed by Mem0 CTO Deshraj, 2025-05-08)
papers.core_idea: Counter-rebuttal: Zep's higher claims allegedly included correct adversarial answers in the numerator while excluding category 5 from the denominator, altered system prompts/retrieval templates, and used a single run; under Mem0's standardized protocol Zep scores 58.44% ± 0.20.
papers.relation_to_qvf: Case study in why LoCoMo numbers are not cross-paper comparable; QVF should publish its exact judge, prompt, category mapping, run count, and per-category counts, and ideally evaluate under multiple harnesses.

papers.title: LoCoMo audit: 6.4% of the answer key is wrong; judge accepts up to 63% of intentionally wrong answers
papers.core_idea: Full audit of locomo10.json: 99/1,540 wrong golden answers (score ceiling ~93.57%), extremely lenient LLM judges (62.81% of vague wrong answers accepted), category 5 (446 Qs) never evaluated in any published result due to eval-code bugs, n=96 open-domain category statistically underpowered, 56% of adjacent leaderboard comparisons statistically indistinguishable, and some vendor scores exceed per-category ceilings (mathematically impossible without credit from wrong gold answers).

papers.title: Benchmarking AI Agent Memory: Is a Filesystem All You Need?
papers.core_idea: A Letta agent that just stores conversation history in files (gpt-4o-mini) scores 74.0% on LoCoMo — beating specialized memory systems — arguing LoCoMo is near-saturated and that memory is about context management, not retrieval machinery.
papers.relation_to_qvf: Sets the bar QVF must beat meaningfully: raw-history baselines already do well on LoCoMo, so QVF's value must show up in temporal/adversarial/multi-hop slices, citation faithfulness, and abstention quality rather than the headline J score.

papers.title: Memobase LoCoMo benchmark (fork of Mem0 evaluation)

papers.title: LoCoMo-MC10: multiple-choice re-release of LoCoMo

papers.title: State of AI Agent Memory 2026 (Mem0 progress report)

benchmark_details: FILE: data/locomo10.json — JSON list of 10 conversation samples. Sample keys: sample_id, qa, conversation, event_summary, observation, session_summary. conversation = {speaker_a, speaker_b, session_<n>: [turns], session_<n>_date_time: "1:56 pm on 8 May, 2023" (natural-language timestamps)}; turn = {speaker, dia_id ("D<session>:<turn>" e.g. "D1:3"), text, optional img_url, blip_caption}. qa item = {question, answer (string|number), evidence: ["D1:3", ...] (ground-truth dia_ids), category: 1–5}; category-5 items carry adversarial_answer instead of answer. SIZES: 10 conversations, ~600 turns and ~26k tokens each (up to 35 sessions); 1,986 QA total; by category number: 1=282, 2=321, 3=96, 4=841, 5=446; non-adversarial = 1,540. CATEGORY TAXONOMY (paper names matched to data numbers): 1=multi-hop (synthesize across sessions; comma-separated multi-part answers), 2=temporal reasoning (dates/durations, needs parsing NL session timestamps), 3=open-domain/counterfactual ("Would X ... if ..."; integrates conversation + world knowledge; only 96 Qs), 4=single-hop (single-session fact; 841 Qs), 5=adversarial (unanswerable; correct behavior is abstaining, originally scored by detecting "no information available"/"not mentioned"). WARNING: the Mem0-lineage harness relabels 1→single_hop, 3→multi_hop, 4→open_domain (only temporal matches the paper) — nearly all post-2025 vendor tables use these swapped labels; disambiguate by counts. METRICS — original repo (task_eval/evaluation.py): normalized token F1 with Porter stemming (articles/punctuation stripped), comma-split partial F1 for category 1, abstention-phrase binary for category 5; also EM, ROUGE-L, BERTScore; retrieval recall@k over 3 RAG DBs (dialogs / observations / session summaries; scripts evaluate_gpts.sh, evaluate_claude.sh, evaluate_gemini.sh, evaluate_hf_llm.sh, evaluate_rag_gpts.sh); event summarization = ROUGE-1/2/L + FactScore; multimodal dialog = MMRelevance (eval code never released). Paper-version stats for reference (50 convs, not released in full): 7,512 QA — single-hop 2,705/multi-hop 1,104/temporal 1,547/open-domain 285/adversarial 1,871; human QA F1 87.9.
